newsitem.title: KENYA: Amnesty accuses Kenya of torturing detainees.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty accuses Kenya of torturing detainees.

text.p: The Kenyan government has failed to halt widespread torture of men, women and children which involves electric shocks and sexual abuse, said human rights group Amnesty International.
It said detainees were tortured by the police, security forces and members of the youth wing of the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party.
The London-based group called on the Kenya Medical Association to publicly condemn torture and any collusion by doctors in its use on detainees.
Amnesty said the Kenyan authorities continued to deny torture charges despite evidence that the practice "is endemic and systematic throughout the country".
"...the Kenyan authorities prefer to deny that these abuses take place and criticise anyone who seeks to publicise them, rather than actually try to remedy the situation," the Amnesty report said.
"In fact, the overwhelming weight of testimony indicates that there is at least one establishment set up specifically to torture opponents of the current government in Kenya," it said.

The Amnesty report came a month after another London-based group -- African Rights -- condemned Kenya's justice system, saying it was collapsing and money and power prevailed in a "shadow" system of injustice which fuelled mob violence.
African Rights said Kenyan justice was corrupt and abusive and that its machinery and ethos had collapsed.
The Amnesty report said conditions inside Kenyan jails were appalling, especially as a result of overcrowding.
"Men and women are kept together; children as young as nine years old have been held with adults and some reportedly raped, and prisoners often have to fight each other for food.
"Victims of torture in Kenya can be men or women, young or old and detained for political or common law offences. The methods used are basic and brutal, sometimes leading to death."

Amnesty said torture involved electric shocks, sexual abuse including rape, the tightening of wire tied around testicles, insertion of objects into the rectum, pricking of genitals with a sharp object, burns, beatings and confinement in the dark.
Amnesty cited the case of an unnamed 19-year old, who was arrested in 1995, and said he was made to hang from a door and was beaten on the soles of his feet.

"The following day interrogators tied a wire around his testicles and pulled for around three minutes. This was repeated several times. The man was then taken back to his cell, where he was seen by a doctor who gave him two Panadol painkillers," it said.
Amnesty gave an example of a woman named Jane Wanbui, five months pregnant at the time of her arrest, who miscarried after a senior police officer kicked her repeatedly in the stomach.
Another woman, 17-year old Virginia Nyambura Wambui, "was whipped and beaten with sticks, kicked and had salt put in her vagina. She was subsequently treated in hospital."

"In some cases the authorities put pressure on health professionals to collaborate in the ill-treatment meted out. On other occasions, doctors' evidence of torture has been rejected or blocked by officials," it said.
The majority of those tortured in Kenya were suspected criminals from the poorest sectors of society, it added.
Amnesty said five prisoners died in custody in 1996 as a result of torture yet no public inquests were held into the deaths.
The rights group called on Kenya's government to take concrete measures to end the widespread torture.

"These should include an end to arbitrary arrest and incommunicado detention, strict controls over interrogation procedures and prohibition of the use of confessions extracted under torture," it said.
